label: Zeus named on Pylos tablets
note: 'di-we' (to Zeus) appears among recipients of offerings on PY Tn 316. This is the name of a god receiving cult, not evidence for the myths of Cronus or the Titanomachy.

label: Hera named beside Zeus at Pylos
note: 'e-ra' receives a gold vessel next to Zeus on PY Tn 316. Whether she was already Zeus' consort is not stated.

label: Poseidon prominent at Pylos
note: 'po-se-da-o' is among the most frequently named deities in the Pylos archive, suggesting he mattered more there than his later Homeric role implies.

label: Hermes on Pylos Tn 316
note: 'e-ma-a2' is read as Hermes. His roles as messenger and trickster are only attested much later, in Homer and the Hymn.

label: Dionysus' name in Linear B
note: 'di-wo-nu-so-jo' (of Dionysus) on Pylos tablets overturned the old view that Dionysus was a late foreign arrival. Nothing in the tablets connects him to wine or Semele.

label: 'Mistress of Atana' at Knossos
note: KN V 52 names 'a-ta-na-po-ti-ni-ja'. Most scholars connect it with Athena, but it may name a place rather than a goddess. Treat as probable, not certain.

label: Cosmic origins first written down
note: Hesiod's Theogony is the earliest surviving text to tell how Chaos, Gaia and the first powers came to be. The cosmogony is recorded here — it does not 'happen' here.

label: The succession myth in Hesiod
note: The overthrow of Uranus by Cronus is first recorded in the Theogony. Close Hurrian-Hittite parallels show that the story pattern existed in the Near East long before Hesiod.

label: The Titanomachy in Hesiod
note: The earliest full narrative of the war of the Titans. A lost epic called the Titanomachy also existed, but only fragments survive.

label: The Trojan War in the Iliad
note: The Iliad is the earliest surviving telling of the war. Its world mixes details from several centuries, so it cannot be read as a report from any single date.

label: The hinge: Troy myth and Hisarlik's ruins
note: This bridge marks the deliberate hinge of MYTHOS. Hisarlik had a large Late Bronze Age city that was destroyed, and Greeks later treated the site as Troy. The archaeology is real; the war of the Iliad is myth. The link records a place where tradition and evidence meet, not proof that the story happened.

label: Odysseus' return in the Odyssey
note: The Odyssey is the first and main record of the wanderings. Every later map of the voyage is an interpretation of this text.

label: Persephone's abduction in the Hymn to Demeter
note: Hesiod mentions the abduction in one line; the Homeric Hymn gives the full story and ties it to Eleusis.

label: Demeter's Mysteries built in stone
note: The Telesterion is physical evidence of the Mysteries. What initiates experienced remained secret, and the myth's relation to the rite is debated.

label: Apollo's oracle, in myth and in the ground
note: The myth of Apollo killing the serpent at Pytho is recorded in the Hymn to Apollo; the sanctuary's growth is visible archaeologically. They are related but separate kinds of evidence.

label: Birth on Delos in the Hymn to Apollo
note: The Hymn to Apollo is the earliest full account of Leto's labour on Delos.

label: Offerings at Olympia
note: Early votives at Olympia mark the beginnings of the sanctuary later dedicated to Zeus. The earliest finds do not name the god.

label: Athena's birth on the Parthenon pediment
note: The east pediment showed Athena's birth from Zeus' head: a myth already told by Hesiod, displayed in civic cult art.

label: Herodotus: poets made the pantheon
note: Herodotus credits Homer and Hesiod with fixing the gods' genealogies and names — an ancient view that the Olympian order was codified by poets.

label: Zeus Ammon: an identification, not an identity
note: Greeks called the Egyptian god Amun 'Zeus Ammon'. This is interpretation by worshippers — two distinct gods with distinct cults were linked, not shown to be the same.

label: Jupiter on the Capitol (interpretatio)
note: Roman Jupiter shares an Indo-European name origin with Zeus and was equated with him by later writers. The Capitoline cult is Roman; MYTHOS shows the link as interpretatio, not identity.

label: Rome pairs twelve gods on the Greek model
note: The lectisternium of twelve gods imitates the Greek Twelve, pairing Roman gods with Greek counterparts. This is a Roman choice of equivalences, not evidence the gods were originally the same.

label: Genealogies systematised in the Bibliotheca
note: The Bibliotheca turns many competing accounts into one reference sequence — useful, but a late compilation, not an original source.

label: End of public cult, survival of myth
note: The edicts end the legal public worship of the Olympians. The myths survive as literature and art: the gods leave the temples but not the stories.
